section_summary: This section contains parts of three monthly political reports prepared by the American Embassy in Tokyo covering Japanese internal affairs and foreign relations from September through November 1937. It records extensive American and foreign diplomatic representations regarding the Sino-Japanese conflict, particularly concerning the safety of foreign nationals, indiscriminate aerial bombardments of civilian institutions, the status of Shanghai's International Settlement, Chinese Maritime Customs revenues, and Japanese salmon fishing off Alaska. It also details Japanese military progress across China, domestic political developments including Cabinet appointments and the Spiritual Mobilization campaign, wartime financial and trade regulations, and diplomatic maneuvers surrounding the Brussels Nine Power Treaty Conference.

subfiles.about: Concluding portion of the American Embassy in Tokyo's monthly report on political, military, legal, and economic conditions in Japan during September 1937.
subfiles.summary: The concluding section of Embassy Despatch No. 2624 (Report No. 132) reviews addresses delivered before the Diet by Premier Hirota and the Ministers of Finance, War, and Navy justifying operations against China and announcing emergency economic policies. It outlines the Cabinet's Spiritual Mobilization program, the court-martial acquittal of General Jinzaburo Mazeki, the sentencing of Dr. Tatsukichi Minobe's assailant, and emergency wartime legislation passed during the 72nd Diet session. The report also assesses emergency military appropriations, gold purchases by the Bank of Japan, foreign trade movements under import-export restrictions, and industrial controls, concluding with schedules of Embassy despatches and telegrams transmitted during September 1937.
subfiles.title: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of September, 1937 (Report No. 132)

subfiles.about: Embassy Despatch No. 2654 transmitting Report No. 133 on political, diplomatic, and economic developments in Japan during October 1937.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits the monthly report for October 1937, reviewing American protests over Japanese air raids on Nanking, Sienhsien, and the Ida Kahn Hospital in Nanchang, as well as the use of Shanghai's International Settlement as a military base. It analyzes Japanese reactions to President Roosevelt's Chicago speech and the League of Nations' condemnation, alongside Japan's refusal to attend the Brussels Nine Power Treaty Conference and strengthening ties with Italy and Germany. The report also examines Japanese military advances in Shanghai and North China, the establishment of the Federated Autonomous Government of Mongolia, Cabinet reorganizations including the appointment of ten temporary counselors, foreign trade controls, and schedules of despatches and telegrams sent during October.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2654: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of October, 1937 (Report No. 133)

subfiles.about: Embassy Despatch No. 2684 transmitting the initial portions of Report No. 134 on Japanese internal conditions and foreign affairs during November 1937.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits the monthly report for November 1937, which continues through the middle of the document on page 533. It documents American representations to preserve the administrative integrity and revenues of the Chinese Maritime Customs in Shanghai, protests against Japanese air attacks on American mission properties in Sungkiang and Wusih, warnings to the population of Soochow, and diplomatic démarches concerning Japanese salmon fishing vessels in Alaskan waters. The report chronicles the capture of Shanghai, Sungkiang, Kiating, Soochow, and Taiyuan, the relocation of the Chinese capital to Chungking, General Matsui's projected peace terms and advance toward Nanking, and the creation of a united autonomous committee for Inner Mongolia and adjacent provinces.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2684: Report on Conditions in Japan During the Month of November, 1937 (Report No. 134)
